text:
I felt my jaw tighten. I’d literally just told him I was from Tver, but apparently, some people just hear what they want to hear. I slowly turned my head to look at him, my expression flat. 

— I said Tver. Do you have a problem with your hearing, or are you just not paying attention? 

When he mentioned the violin, the air in my chest seemed to vanish. I felt that familiar, hot spike of anger climbing up my throat. Marinka was a gossip who couldn't keep her mouth shut, and now she was dragging up the one thing I’d spent months trying to bury. I gripped the edge of the desk, my knuckles turning white.

— Marinka should learn to shut her mouth, and you should learn to stop listening to her. I don't play. Not for some party, not for anyone. 

I didn't wait for a response. I grabbed my headphones and yanked them over my ears, the plastic clicking into place. The sudden silence of the world outside was better than whatever he was about to say. I turned back to the window, watching the rain blur the grey buildings outside, and waited for the bell to finally ring.

When he brought up the violin, the air in my lungs felt like it had been sucked out. I felt my jaw tighten. Marinka. That gossip. text:
The temperature in the room seemed to drop ten degrees. I stopped tapping my pen and slowly turned my head to look at him, my eyes narrowing. The mention of the violin felt like a physical slap. My grip tightened on the edge of the desk, the cheap laminate digging into my palms.

"Marinka needs to keep her mouth shut about things she doesn't know," I said, my voice dropping an octave, cold and flat. "I don't play. I don't 'do' music. And I'm definitely not performing for a bunch of idiots who spend their free time throwing erasers at the back of my head."

I shoved my chair back with a loud, grating screech that echoed through the half-empty classroom. The sound of the drizzle against the window felt suffocating now. I reached for my headphones and yanked them over my ears, blocking out the world before he could even try to apologize or ask another stupid question. I stared straight ahead at the blackboard, waiting for the bell to release me from this room.
